item.title: ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers [1] (NAACL 2024), Chaitanya Malaviya and co-authors (Penn + UW) build a 2,177-question benchmark of information-seeking prompts authored by 484 domain experts across 32 fields, then have the same experts judge responses from attribution-generating language-model systems on factuality, citeworthiness, and source reliability.

As language models are adopted by a more sophisticated and diverse set of users, the importance of guaranteeing that they provide factually correct information supported by verifiable sources is critical across fields of study. This is especially the case for high-stakes fields, such as medicine and law, where the risk of propagating false information is high and can lead to undesirable societal consequences. Previous work studying attribution and factuality has not focused on analyzing these characteristics of language model outputs in domain-specific scenarios. In this work, we conduct human evaluation of responses from a few representative systems along various axes of attribution and factuality, by bringing domain experts in the loop. Specifically, we collect expert-curated questions from 484 participants across 32 fields of study, and then ask the same experts to evaluate generated responses to their own questions. In addition, we ask experts to improve upon responses from language models. The output of our analysis is ExpertQA, a high-quality long-form QA dataset with 2177 questions spanning 32 fields, along with verified answers and attributions for claims in the answers.

Methods

The protocol puts experts in the loop twice. First, 484 experts across 32 fields (medicine, law, engineering, humanities, social sciences) write information-seeking questions they would genuinely want answered in their own professional work, producing 2,177 questions. Each author tags every question with one or more of seven information-need types:

  • Directed (Type I): a question with a single, unambiguous answer.
  • Open-ended (Type II): potentially ambiguous, admitting several valid answers.
  • Summarization (Type III): a request to summarize what is known on a topic.
  • Advice (Type IV): suggestions on how to approach a problem.
  • Hypothetical (Type V): a question built on a described scenario, and the most common type, since experts were asked to write two of their five questions this way.
  • List of resources (Type VI): a request for a list of places to find more information.
  • Opinion (Type VII): a request for an opinion on a topic.

The results lean on this taxonomy. Second, each question is answered by six attributed-answer configurations:

  • Closed-book GPT-4, prompted to answer from parametric memory and cite supporting URLs, with no retrieval.
  • Retrieve-then-read (rr): retrieve evidence first, then generate the answer with GPT-4, over two corpora: Google Search (rr_gs) and the static Sphere corpus (rr_sphere), a web-scale subset of Common Crawl [4] retrieved with BM25.
  • Post-hoc attribution (post_hoc): generate the answer first, then retrieve a citation for each claim as a separate step, again over Google Search (post_hoc_gs) and Sphere (post_hoc_sphere).
  • BingChat (bing_chat), a commercial retrieval-augmented system, sampled in balanced mode.

Grading happens at two granularities. An answer is the complete response a system returns to a question. Each answer is split into claims: sentence-level units (segmented with spaCy), each paired with whatever evidence the system cited for it. Only one of the six Likert axes judges the whole answer: answer usefulness, whether the complete response addresses the question. The other five judge individual claims and their evidence: three about the claim itself (factuality, informativeness, cite-worthiness) and two about its attribution (claim/evidence support, scored complete / partial / incomplete, and source reliability). Finally, the expert revises each claim and its evidence so the answer is factual and fully supported, yielding an expert-verified reference answer set.

Results

  • Every system leaves a large share of claims unsupported, even when the answer is fluent and authoritative: across systems, many claims are uncited, contradicted by the cited evidence, or backed by low-reliability sources.
  • Retrieve-then-read and post-hoc attribution fail differently. Retrieve-then-read produces more complete attributions but misses citations for some cite-worthy claims (about 18% go uncited). Post-hoc systems return a citation for every claim by design, yet more of those citations are incomplete, because retrieving without the answer’s context is harder.
  • Closed-book GPT-4 cites plausible-but-wrong pages. Without retrieval it generates citations to believable domains (nasa.gov for astronomy, nih.gov for medicine), but the linked page fails to support the claim more than 60% of the time.
  • The retrieval corpus drives source reliability. Sphere returns unreliable evidence (a blog comment retrieved for a breast-cancer question). Switching to Google Search raises the reliability experts assign to the evidence.
  • High-stakes fields fare worst on attribution. Most claims are judged factually correct (over 85% in many fields) and cite-worthy (only about 17–22% are judged not cite-worthy), but medicine and law show roughly 35% and 31% unsupported claims, and about 51% of medical claims cite sources experts rate as not reliable.
  • Requests for a list of resources (Type VI) break systems hardest, with advice (Type IV) and opinion (Type VII) questions close behind. Claims to these are the least informative, factual, and well-supported. Separately, 30–40% of claims across systems are low-relevance “void” claims that mostly restate the question or state simplistic facts.

The paper also breaks the grades down by field and by question type, which is where the more interesting structure shows up.

  • Question-type composition is field-specific (Figure 8). The mix of the seven types swings widely across fields: physics and astronomy lean toward directed, single-answer questions, while several fields’ bars cover only a subset of the seven types at all, some as few as four. Type V (hypothetical) is the largest slice almost everywhere, inflated by construction because experts were asked to write two of their five questions that way.
  • The per-field view yields few clear cross-field patterns (Figure 9). Factuality stays high across most fields (the paper notes Definitely- or Probably-correct rates above 85% in many of them), and it reports no clean ranking emerging from the field-level trends.
  • Difficulty tracks question type (Figure 10). Type VI (list-of-resources) falls at the low end of almost every property. The paper flags advice (Type IV) and opinion (Type VII) as the next hardest, with claims to all three judged less informative, factual, and well-supported than the directed and open-ended types.

My Notes

  • Having the same expert author and grade the response fixes a selection problem FActScore sidesteps. Prior factuality benchmarks either use crowdworkers on generic prompts or use automated metrics against a canonical source (Wikipedia for biographies, as in FActScore [2]). Both fail in specialist domains because the questions themselves are not representative of what experts actually ask, and the “knowledge source” for medicine or law has no clean Wikipedia analog. Having the same expert author the question and grade the response closes the loop that makes ELI5- or TriviaQA-style benchmarks under-diagnose domain failures.

  • Post-hoc attribution is the more informative of the two orderings tested, and it does worse. ExpertQA tests two sequential orderings: retrieve-then-generate, and generate-then-retrieve (post-hoc, where the answer is written first and evidence is fetched per claim afterward). Post-hoc is the worse of the two: its fluent answers often make claims no retrieved source actually supports. But that decides ordering, not architecture: neither system interleaves retrieval and generation, so whether interleaving (as in Self-RAG [3]) would beat both is our own speculation, untested here.

  • A field’s difficulty partly reflects what it asks as much as how well it is served. Read together, Figures 8 and 10 line up: question-type composition varies sharply by field, and difficulty tracks question type, with Type VI (list-of-resources) and the advice and opinion types at the low end of nearly every property. A field weighted toward those types would post weaker claim-level numbers even if the underlying systems were no worse there. Among the larger fields, that hard-question share is heaviest in economics, education, history, literature, and visual arts (several of which do score at the bottom on usefulness or attribution), while physics and astronomy has almost none of them. The benchmark doesn’t separate the two effects (it reports type and field independently, not field scores adjusted for question mix), so this stays a reading of the breakdowns rather than something the paper isolates, but it argues against ranking fields on raw claim scores.

  • What each field never asks (Figure 8, enumerated from the released data). Eight of the 32 fields skip at least one of the seven types entirely, all of them small fields, so the gaps reflect how questions were collected more than the disciplines:

    • No list-of-resources (VI): journalism, mathematics, philosophy, culinary arts, theology. The rarest type overall, so it drops out first.
    • No opinion (VII): classical studies, criminology, theology.
    • No advice (IV): climate science, culinary arts.
    • No summarization (III): culinary arts, theology.
    • Most lopsided: theology and culinary arts each span only four of the seven types.

  • Recomputing the grades sharpens the type story and undercuts the field one. Scoring each Likert axis on a 0–1 scale over the released annotations (my mapping, not the paper’s category counts):

    • By question type the order is stable across axes: directed questions (Type I) score highest almost everywhere and list-of-resources (VI) lowest, with advice and opinion just above it, on usefulness, factuality, informativeness, and cite-worthiness alike.
    • Two axes break the pattern: source reliability is essentially flat (~0.74 for every type), and attribution is the lowest-scoring axis overall (0.59–0.68 across types). So a “hard” question type is one whose claims are less informative, factual, and cite-worthy, not one whose sources are worse.
    • By field, extremes appear but are confounded: usefulness is highest for mathematics, anthropology, and the military/law-enforcement field, lowest for education, history, and literature. Attribution is best in anthropology and architecture, worst in economics and literature. But each question was graded for a single sampled system, so a field’s average folds in which system happened to answer there, and several fields rest on twenty-odd answers, so these field rankings shouldn’t be read at face value.

References

  1. Malaviya, C., Lee, S., Chen, S., Sieber, E., Yatskar, M., Roth, D.. “ExpertQA: Expert-Curated Questions and Attributed Answers.” NAACL 2024, arXiv:2309.07852, Sep 14, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07852
  2. Min, S., Krishna, K., Lyu, X., Lewis, M., Yih, W.-t., Koh, P. W., Iyyer, M., Zettlemoyer, L., Hajishirzi, H.. “FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation.” EMNLP 2023, arXiv:2305.14251. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14251
  3. Asai, A., Wu, Z., Wang, Y., Sil, A., Hajishirzi, H.. “Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection.” ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.11511. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11511
  4. Piktus, A., Petroni, F., Karpukhin, V., Okhonko, D., Broscheit, S., Izacard, G., Lewis, P., Oğuz, B., Grave, E., Yih, W.-t., Riedel, S. “The Web Is Your Oyster — Knowledge-Intensive NLP Against a Very Large Web Corpus.” arXiv:2112.09924, Dec 2021. https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.09924

Related Posts

  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: the constructive complement — where ExpertQA measures attribution failure, this gives statistical guarantees on which claims to keep.
  • AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 Queries: the focused legal-domain version of ExpertQA’s finding that law and medicine fare worst on attribution.
  • TruthfulQA: Are Larger LLMs More Truthful?: an earlier factuality benchmark that ExpertQA pushes into expert domains and pairs with claim-level attribution.
  • TWEAK at NAACL 2024: Decoding Without Hallucinations: a same-venue take on the same attribution problem, working at decode time rather than as a post-hoc step.
  • RAG with Knowledge Graphs: Key Open Questions: the retrieval side of the retrieve-then-read and post-hoc systems ExpertQA evaluates.

item.title: AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions [1] (arXiv preprint, March 2026), Field, S., Douglas, R., and Krueger, D. (the ML Alignment and Theory Scholars Program, Berkeley) interview 25 frontier-lab and academic AI researchers and find converging predictions on a path to autonomous AI developers, paired with a sharp epistemic split on timelines, deployment, and governance.

Many leading AI researchers expect AI development to exceed the transformative impact of all previous technological revolutions. This belief is based on the idea that AI will be able to automate the process of AI research itself, leading to a positive feedback loop. In August and September of 2025, we interviewed 25 leading researchers from frontier AI labs and academia, including participants from Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, UC Berkeley, Princeton, and Stanford to understand researcher perspectives on these scenarios. Though AI systems have not yet been able to recursively improve, 20 of the 25 researchers interviewed identified automating AI research as one of the most severe and urgent AI risks. Participants converged on predictions that AI agents will become more capable at coding, math and eventually AI development, gradually transitioning from ‘assistants’ or ‘tools’ to ‘autonomous AI developers,’ after which point, predictions diverge. While researchers agreed upon the possibility of recursive improvement, they disagreed on basic questions of timelines or appropriate governance mechanisms. For example, an epistemic divide emerged between frontier lab researchers and academic researchers, the latter of which expressed more skepticism about explosive growth scenarios. Additionally, 17/25 participants expected AI systems with advanced coding or R&D capabilities to be increasingly reserved for internal use at AI companies or governments, unseen by the public. The concerns most frequently raised by participants were power concentration and AI-augmented progress accelerating behind closed doors, and they offered different suggestions for mitigation strategies or explanations for why certain mitigations might turn out worse than the problem they seek to solve. Participants were split as to whether setting regulatory ‘red lines’ was a good idea, though almost all favored transparency-based mitigations.

Methods

The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 25 AI researchers conducted in August and September 2025. Participants were recruited from frontier AI labs (Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta) and academia (UC Berkeley, Princeton, Stanford), with selection prioritizing diversity of perspectives among researchers with published work on recursive improvement or comparable capability forecasting. The interview protocol covers three sections:

  • Conceptualizing ASARA (“AI Systems for AI R&D Automation,” the paper’s operational term for systems that can meaningfully contribute to frontier-AI development): what such a system would look like.
  • Organizational dynamics: how labs would deploy such systems.
  • Risk and governance: risk assessment plus governance preferences.

Transcripts are qualitatively coded for themes. Participant affiliations span five types (frontier-lab, ex-frontier-lab, academic, industry, and nonprofit), used to show where opinions cluster and where they diverge.

Results

The paper organizes findings around five themes:

  • what participants imagine ASARA looking like
  • public versus internal deployment
  • trajectory clarity
  • risk perception
  • views on red lines

The findings, with the figures that ground them:

  • Severe-and-urgent risk: 20/25. Twenty of the 25 participants identified automating AI research as one of the most severe and urgent AI risks. The two most-frequently raised concerns were power concentration and AI-augmented progress accelerating behind closed doors. The most common specific worry, in 18 of 25 transcripts, was that recursive self-improvement amplifies every other AI risk at once. Figure 3 sorts participants by how they rank ASARA risk, from minimal concern through serious risk to the primary driver of AI risk, and groups them by affiliation. Most fall in the serious-to-primary range, with academics the affiliation most represented at the minimal-concern end.

  • Internal-only deployment: 17/25. Seventeen participants expected ASARA-class systems to be increasingly reserved for internal use at AI companies or governments rather than publicly deployed (Figure 1, the cover image). Reasons offered include too-valuable-to-share, higher returns from internal R&D than from API revenue, and competitive dynamics.

  • Trajectory clarity by affiliation. Figure 2 places each participant on a spectrum from “Clear Path” through “Major Obstacles” to “Unknown/Unknowns.” Frontier-lab researchers cluster toward “Clear Path,” while academic researchers spread across the spectrum, with several identifying “Major Obstacles” and no participant in the “Unknown/Unknowns” category. Section 4.1 names this “Schism Between Silicon Valley and Academia.”

  • Red lines: split. Transparency: near-universal. Participants divided on whether regulatory “red lines” (limits whose breach should trigger major response by labs or governments) were a good idea. Figure 4 shows the split between favoring, being unsure about, and opposing red lines, roughly balanced across affiliations. Concrete objections include definitional ambiguity, enforcement difficulty, and a fear that lines drawn at the wrong threshold could backfire by promoting workarounds. Almost all participants favored transparency-based mitigations as either complement or alternative.

References

  1. Field, S., Douglas, R., and Krueger, D.. “AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2603.03338), March 5, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03338

Related Posts

  • Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?: the outside-view forecast this paper’s interviews sit next to, putting a 60% number on the automation scenario the participants describe.
  • Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI: a funded company chasing the internal, self-improving endpoint that 17 of 25 participants expect.
  • Superintelligence: The Idea That Eats Smart People: the skeptic’s counterweight to the intelligence-explosion premise nearly all the interviewees take seriously.
  • Update: Karpathy’s ‘AGI Is Still a Decade Away’ — Karpathy Joins Anthropic: a concrete version of the timeline skepticism the academic participants voiced.
  • OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI: a frontier lab’s own governance commitments, against which the participants’ red-lines-versus-transparency split reads.

item.title: Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression [1] (ECML 2002), Harris Papadopoulos, Kostas Proedrou, Vladimir Vovk, and Alexander Gammerman (Royal Holloway, University of London) replace the per-test-point retraining of the original confidence-machine construction [2] with a single training run plus a held-out calibration set. The result is regression prediction intervals that keep the same validity guarantee at much lower computational cost. This is the paper that introduced what the field now calls inductive (or split) conformal prediction.

The paper contrasts two constructions and replaces the first with the second:

  • Transductive Confidence Machine (TCM): the original construction (Gammerman, Vapnik, and Vovk [2]). To test a candidate label for a new object, refit the underlying algorithm with that label added to the training set and measure how unusual the object looks against the rest. It is valid, but it retrains once per candidate label, and every test example restarts the computation from scratch. For regression the label is a real number, so there is no finite set of candidates to sweep cleanly.
  • Inductive Confidence Machine (ICM): train the underlying algorithm once on a proper training set, set the remaining labeled examples aside as a calibration set, and build the predictive region for a new object directly from the calibration residuals. One training run, no per-test refitting, and the same coverage guarantee.

The existing methods of predicting with confidence give good accuracy and confidence values, but quite often are computationally inefficient. Some partial solutions have been suggested in the past. Both the original method and these solutions were based on transductive inference. In this paper we make a radical step of replacing transductive inference with inductive inference and define what we call the Inductive Confidence Machine (ICM); our main concern in this paper is the use of ICM in regression problems. The algorithm proposed in this paper is based on the Ridge Regression procedure (which is usually used for outputting bare predictions) and is much faster than the existing transductive techniques. The inductive approach described in this paper may be the only option available when dealing with large data sets.

Methods

The underlying algorithm is Ridge Regression (RR), the linear least-squares fit with an penalty, trained once on the proper training set; call the fitted predictor the rule (the paper’s decision rule). Each calibration example then gets a strangeness measure (the paper’s term for what is now called a nonconformity score), a number measuring how poorly the trained rule predicts it. The simplest choice is the absolute residual , where is the rule’s prediction.

To form a predictive region at confidence level for a new object ( is the significance level, the allowed probability of the region missing the true label; e.g.  for a 95% region), ICM proceeds in three steps:

  • Score each candidate label. Rank the new object’s strangeness against the calibration scores through a p-value, , counting over the calibration scores and the new object’s score. The predictive region is every label whose p-value exceeds .
  • Read the region off in closed form. With the absolute-residual score there is no need to test labels one by one. Clearing the denominator in the keep-rule turns it into a count threshold, : since is a fraction of the scores, is a rank. So sort the calibration residuals in descending order and take the -th largest, (the floor snaps down to the nearest level the scores can represent, a multiple of ) — a candidate survives unless it lands among the strangest scores. The region is the point prediction plus or minus that residual, : the same keep-if- filter, with the continuum of candidate labels collapsed to a single interval.
  • Interpret the cutoff. is essentially the empirical quantile of the calibration residuals — with the paper’s calibration examples, a 95% interval () uses the 5th-largest residual, and a 99% interval uses the largest.

Because the calibration scores and the new object’s score are exchangeable under the paper’s i.i.d. assumption, the true label falls inside the region with probability at least , for any underlying regressor and any sample size, with no distributional assumptions [3]. It is the same exchangeability argument the conformal-prediction primer makes for classification, applied to a continuous label. The overhead over plain RR is light: the rule is fit once, scored on the calibration set once, and each test point needs only one application of the rule.

The constant measure — the absolute residual above — hands every test object the same interval half-width, which is uninformative. The paper’s second score, the normalized measure, divides the residual by an estimate of how hard the object is to predict, , with . The difficulty estimate comes from a second ridge regression. Label the rule RR1 and this difficulty model RR2; RR2 trains after RR1:

  • Fit RR1, then record its errors. Train RR1 on the proper training set, feed each proper-training example back through it, and record the log absolute error .
  • Fit RR2 on those errors. Train RR2 on the pairs (features, log error) to predict how far off RR1 will be; its output gives (the keeps positive).
  • Keep both, don’t swap. At prediction time RR1 centers the interval and supplies the numerator ; RR2 supplies the per-object difficulty in the denominator. Both are one-time fits — still no per-test retraining.

The interval width then scales with predicted difficulty: narrower where RR is accurate, wider where it is not. This is the regression analog of set size in classification: interval width is how the method reports uncertainty.

The contrast is visible in the distribution of interval widths. Within one data split every test object gets the identical interval, with zero object-to-object spread. Note that in Figure 1, two different concepts of “width” are illustrated, and they should not be conflated. A box’s position on the Region width scale is the prediction-region width itself, which rises with confidence: smaller → higher confidence level → a wider interval (≈9.5, ≈12, ≈15.5 at the 90/95/99% confidence levels, which the paper loosely terms accuracy level). A box’s height is second-order: that’s the split-to-split spread of that one width across the 100 random partitions (median, quartiles, 10th/90th percentiles), since each split draws a different calibration set and so a different . The boxes stay short because that second-order spread is small; they grow a little taller at higher confidence because is read off a more extreme, more variable tail of the residuals — at 99% it is the single largest of the 99. Figure 2 (the cover, the normalized measure with RR2’s in the denominator) makes the contrast clear: the box positions climb with confidence just as in Figure 1, and the medians are nearly identical — the first-order trend is unchanged — but the boxes are now much taller. That added height is the adaptivity: the width now varies across test objects within a single split, wide where RR is expected to err and narrow where it is not, so the box height reflects genuine object-to-object spread rather than the tiny split-to-split wobble of Figure 1.

Results

The paper tests ICM with Ridge Regression on the Boston Housing data set (506 examples, house values from 5K to 50K, 13 attributes), averaged over 100 random splits into a 382-example proper training set, a 99-example calibration set, and a 25-example test set. Two larger sets, Bank Rejection and CPU Activity (8,192 examples each), check that it scales. Three kernels are tried with RR: polynomial, RBF, and ANOVA splines.

The findings:

  • Empirical coverage matches the guarantee: the fraction of intervals containing the true label is at or above the nominal 90%, 95%, and 99% levels in every setting but one, where ANOVA splines reach 98.8% at the 99% level (Table 1). That confirms the validity proof on real data.
  • The speedup barely costs any interval tightness: ICM’s win over TCM is computational — one fit instead of recomputing per query — so the real question is how much sharpness it gives up for that. On width the answer is almost none: ICM beats the first TCM variant outright on mean width and trails the second on median width only at 90–95%, edging ahead at 99% (Tables 5 and 6), despite training on fewer examples and ranking against a shorter list of strangeness scores.
  • At matched confidence levels, the normalized measure’s typical interval is about as tight — slightly tighter at high confidence: comparing median widths between the two measures at the same level, the normalized one is about even at 90% and a touch smaller at 95% and 99% (for ANOVA splines, 11.7 and 15.0 versus 12.2 and 15.4). This is separate from the taller boxes of Figure 2: those show the across-object spread, this the median interval. The normalized measure keeps the typical interval about as tight while redistributing width toward the hard objects. ANOVA splines gave the best results.
  • The intervals are informative, not just valid: the best configuration covers the true Boston Housing price within a band spanning only 33% of the full price range at 99% confidence.

My Notes

  • This is where conformal prediction became practical: the primer credits its later spread to being repackaged as a few lines of code against a frozen model — and that frozen-model recipe is the inductive construction introduced here. The “confidence machine” name did not survive, but the method became standard, now usually called split or inductive conformal prediction (ICP).
  • The trade that made the method last: ICM gives up a little. The regressor trains on fewer examples, and the attainable confidence levels are coarser (the achievable significance levels are only multiples of , set by the calibration size ). In exchange it does one fit instead of a fresh computation per query. The paper shows the statistical loss is minor. The deeper reason the inductive form won is that the transductive form simply does not run at modern dataset sizes, and the compute argument has only gotten stronger in the twenty years since.
  • The normalized measure is a learned error model: its comes from RR2, trained to predict RR1’s log error — the interval width becomes a small model of where the predictor fails, bolted onto the predictor. Because validity rests on the calibration set’s exchangeability, can be any function without touching coverage; it changes only sharpness, how width is shared out across inputs. That is what enabled everything that came later in conformal regression (locally adaptive residuals, per-group calibration, quantile-based variants): a better answer to the question this paper raised — not whether the interval is valid, which it always is, but whether its width can match the real difficulty of each input.
  • The difficulty estimate is fit in-sample, so it skews optimistic: RR2 trains on RR1’s residuals over the very examples RR1 was fit on, where errors run smaller than on fresh inputs. So understates difficulty and the resulting widths track training error rather than test error — which, by the point above, dents sharpness but not coverage. A cleaner design would estimate the errors out-of-fold.

References

  1. Papadopoulos, H., Proedrou, K., Vovk, V., and Gammerman, A. “Inductive Confidence Machines for Regression.” Proceedings of the 13th European Conference on Machine Learning (ECML 2002), Lecture Notes in Computer Science vol. 2430, pp. 345–356. Springer, 2002. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-36755-1_29
  2. Gammerman, A., Vapnik, V., and Vovk, V. “Learning by Transduction.” Proceedings of the 14th Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 1998), pp. 148–156, 1998.
  3. Vovk, V., Gammerman, A., and Shafer, G. Algorithmic Learning in a Random World. Springer, 2005. https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b106715

Related Posts

  • Transduction with Confidence and Credibility: the transductive predecessor this paper replaces, where the SVM is refit under every candidate label rather than trained once against a calibration set.
  • Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness: the theory paper for that same transductive construction, whose §6 regression impossibility this paper sidesteps by returning intervals rather than point estimates.
  • A Primer on Conformal Prediction: the modern account that credits conformal prediction’s spread to exactly the frozen-model, split construction introduced here.
  • Conformal Language Modeling: a language-model method built on the split-conformal recipe this paper made practical.
  • Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: another LLM application of the inductive conformal machinery this paper introduced.

item.title: Benchmarks in Leipzig
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Benchmarks in Leipzig [1], Christian Stump (Ruhr University Bochum), Veronica Calvo Cortes, and Bernd Sturmfels (Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences, Leipzig), with 46 other mathematicians, present a benchmark of 100 research-level math questions with short, known answers and report how far current frontier models get on it.

Between April 1 and May 15, 2026, a group of 49 mathematicians compiled a dataset of research-level mathematics questions with known answers. Most of the work was done during the 3-day workshop Benchmarks in Leipzig with 35 participants at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences in Leipzig, Germany. We present the resulting collection of 100 questions. We evaluated these questions in three stages: a single attempt by five state-of-the-art LLMs, followed by a 20-runs-per-model evaluation with three of these models, and finally a 3-run attempt with two heavy-thinking models. After Stage 1, 41 questions remained completely unsolved; after Stage 2, this count dropped to 16; and we concluded Stage 3 with only 2 unsolved questions. This demonstrates that the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs are becoming impressive.

Methods

The benchmark was built by 49 mathematicians, with most of the work happening during a three-day workshop (May 11–13, 2026) with 35 participants at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences in Leipzig. The project began at the Combinatorial Coworkspace in March 2026 and runs on the ScienceBench platform, where contributors submit questions, browse and comment on each other’s, and query all the project’s models from a shared chat interface.

Each question had to meet a short set of guidelines:

  • Unique, well-defined, unguessable answer: the answer is short and checkable, and a reader who guesses repeatedly without working out the details should have no realistic chance of getting it right.
  • Grounded in public research, but beyond it: questions build on existing, publicly accessible work but go past what a paper itself states, and the solution cannot depend on non-public results.
  • Hard to guess in practice was the tricky part: several submissions turned out to have only a few possible answers, and were reworked or dropped.

Submissions then went through an audit. Before any model attempted a question, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro checked it against the guidelines. Every contributor could see all questions alongside the models’ answers and solutions, and comparing submissions against model-generated solutions led to 12 reformulated questions and 3 removed from the set. The final 100 questions skew heavily toward the contributors’ own fields (Table 1, the cover): 36 in algebraic geometry, then algebraic combinatorics (22), matroid theory (18), representation theory (15), and enumerative combinatorics (15), with a long tail of smaller areas. The authors generated that area breakdown with Claude Opus 4.7 and then verified it by hand.

Results

The 100 questions were run through three evaluation stages, with a question counted as “solved” if at least one model run produced the correct answer:

  • Stage 1 (single attempt): five project-active models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Grok 4.3) and their immediate predecessors each got one try per question during submission.
  • Stage 2 (20 runs): Surge AI queried three of the models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7) 20 times on each question.
  • Stage 3 (heavy thinking): GPT-5.5 Pro with Extended Thinking (3 runs, via ChatGPT) and Gemini 3.1 Pro Deep Think (3 runs, via Surge AI).

The unsolved count shrinks across the three stages: 41 after Stage 1, 16 after Stage 2, and just 2 after Stage 3. The per-stage detail:

  • Single attempt favors one model: GPT-5.5 solved 44 of 100 on one try, the next best (Gemini 3.1 Pro) managed 15, and Grok 4.3 just 6 (Table 2). Predecessor models trailed their successors in most cases.
  • More samples close most of the gap: with 20 runs each, GPT-5.5 solved 75 of 100 (52% of its 2,000 attempts correct), Gemini 3.1 Pro 40 (20%), and Claude Opus 4.7 44 (15%) (Table 3).
  • Heavy-thinking modes close almost all of it: GPT-5.5 Pro with Extended Thinking answered every one of its 300 runs, got 79% right, and solved 88 of 100, while Gemini 3.1 Pro Deep Think solved 56 (Table 4).
  • First-solved breakdown: 59 questions were first cracked in Stage 1, 25 more in Stage 2, 14 in Stage 3, leaving 2 unsolved.

Per-question consistency differs by model (Table 6). GPT-5.5 is bimodal: it got every attempt wrong on 25 questions and every attempt right on 27, with relatively few in between. For the other two models, correct answers spread more thinly across the 20 runs, with more questions solved on only a handful of attempts.

My Notes

  • The benchmark already saturates at the top: the abstract calls the results a sign that “the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs are becoming impressive,” but the body’s first key finding is blunter. The exercise-style recipe (questions drawn from published research with a short checkable answer) has “reached its limits” for the best models, which solve almost all of them: GPT-5.5 Pro with Extended Thinking got 88 of the 100 (Table 4). The method still separates weaker models, but the limit is difficulty rather than supply: more questions of the same kind would not be hard enough to measure the frontier.

  • The solve count overstates repeatable ability: a question counts as solved on one correct run out of twenty, so the headline totals treat a reliable answer and a one-in-twenty fluke the same. The per-question distribution (Table 6) shows how far apart the two can be. GPT-5.5 is bimodal: wrong on all 20 runs for 25 questions and right on all 20 for 27, with little in between. Across the three models, many solved questions were answered correctly on only one to four of the twenty runs, so much of the solve count rests on inconsistent, sometimes lucky, results.

  • The questions are built to resist contamination: three features keep these question and answer pairs out of the models’ training data. They are new, written in April and May 2026, after the evaluated checkpoints were frozen (Gemini 3.1 Pro shipped March 17, GPT-5.5 April 23), so the pairs did not exist when the models were trained. They are unpublished by design, each made to go beyond what would fit in a paper, so the specific question and answer are not online to scrape. And the answer key was shown to neither the models nor the other contributors. A model saw only the question. The one thing this does not rule out, deliberately, is the models having learned the public results the solutions build on, but that is the capability being tested rather than leakage.

References

  1. Stump, C., Calvo Cortes, V., Sturmfels, B., and 46 others. “Benchmarks in Leipzig: A Collection of Questions in Research-Level Mathematics.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.05818), June 4, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05818

Related Posts

  • Mapping Benchmark Creation and Saturation in AI: the create-then-saturate pattern this benchmark already shows, a fresh research-math set nearly solved by frontier models.
  • Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search: the verification-backed alternative, settling open problems with machine-checked Lean proofs rather than grading against a known answer.
  • An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture: a single high-profile instance of the research-math capability this benchmark measures across 100 questions.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the argument that trustworthy LLM math needs a deterministic verifier, relevant when a solve can be a one-in-twenty fluke.
  • The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics: names training-data contamination and unverifiable AI math claims as threats that this benchmark’s post-cutoff, hidden-answer design is built to resist.

item.title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), George Tsoukalas, Anton Kovsharov, Sergey Shirobokov, and 15 colleagues at Google DeepMind and Aarhus University — with Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri as corresponding authors — report the first large-scale evaluation of LLM-driven formal proof search on open mathematical problems.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly excel at mathematical reasoning, but their unreliability limits their utility in mathematics research. A mitigation is using LLMs to generate formal proofs in languages like Lean. We perform the first large-scale evaluation of this method’s ability to solve open problems. Our most capable agent autonomously resolved 9 of 353 open Erdős problems at the per-problem cost of a few hundred dollars, proved 44/492 OEIS conjectures, and is being deployed in combinatorics, optimization, graph theory, algebraic geometry, and quantum optics research. A basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes but proved costlier on the hardest problems. These findings demonstrate the power of AI-aided formal proof search and shed light on the agent designs that enable it.

Methods

AlphaProof Nexus is a framework for agents that query two things in a loop: a frontier LLM that proposes mathematics, and the Lean compiler that checks it. In Lean, definitions, theorems, and proofs are all mechanically verified code. A proof is built from tactics, elementary steps the compiler runs one at a time while tracking the goals still left to prove, and it is complete only when no goals remain. Lean also has a sorry tactic that closes any goal while still passing the type-checker, so proving a theorem reduces to a concrete coding task: rewrite the file until it compiles with no sorry left.

The agent’s input is a proof sketch: a Lean file holding the target theorem, the definitions and library imports it depends on, and sorry where the proof should go. The mathematician can add natural-language context and domain knowledge encoded in Lean, and marks which parts of the file the agent may edit, with EVOLVE-BLOCK regions where it can introduce helper lemmas, definitions, and proof steps, and EVOLVE-VALUE regions enclosing parameters whose values it may change. On success the agent returns a sorry-free proof.

The paper builds four agents on this framework and tests them in four combinations:

  • (A) Basic generate-and-verify. A set of prover subagents run independently with no shared state. Each is a “Ralph loop”: a sequence of episodes, where an episode is a multi-turn Gemini 3.1 Pro inference loop that reasons step by step and edits the sketch with a search-and-replace tool. After each turn the subagent compiles the sketch. A Lean error message becomes the instruction for the next turn. If an episode ends with a sorry still in the file, the subagent writes a comment summarizing what it learned, and that annotated sketch seeds the next episode.
  • (B) Basic plus AlphaProof. The prover can hand an unproved goal to AlphaProof, DeepMind’s reinforcement-learning prover for Olympiad-level Lean. AlphaProof returns a proof, which is substituted straight into the sketch, a disproof showing the goal is false, or a failure message. Disproofs and failures are fed back into the prover’s prompt.
  • (C) Basic plus evolution. Prover subagents draw from and contribute to a shared population of validated sketches, in the style of DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve. Formal proof is pass-or-fail, which leaves an evolutionary search nothing to climb, so a pool of cheaper Gemini 3.0 Flash rater subagents ranks sketches by plausibility, clarity, and novelty: an LLM critic compares them in pairwise matches, the results become Elo scores, and a selection rule from Monte Carlo tree search (P-UCB, which favors high-scoring sketches while still exploring less-tried ones) decides which to evolve next.
  • (D) Full-featured. Combines AlphaProof and evolutionary search, and is the agent used for the paper’s main results.

A validator checks every result before it counts, confirming that the final sketch compiles and that the agent did not quietly weaken the theorem statement to make the proof easier.

Results

The evaluation covers 353 open Erdős problems and 492 conjectures from the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), with a focused cost comparison run on six Erdős instances. The metric is solve rate against mean inference cost in dollars, swept over independent attempts. The prover is Gemini 3.1 Pro and the rater Gemini 3.0 Flash. Reported costs exclude AlphaProof’s own inference (estimated around $60 per problem), which the authors note does not change the comparison.

The findings:

  • Nine of 353 open Erdős problems solved by the full-featured agent (D), including two that had been open for 56 years, at a few hundred dollars per problem.
  • Forty-four of 492 OEIS conjectures proved.
  • The basic agent (A) solved all nine Erdős problems too, at higher cost on the hardest ones. On most problems (A) or (B) sat on the cost–performance Pareto frontier, and the full-featured (D) pulled ahead only on the hardest, such as Erdős #125.
  • Already in use in active research across optimization theory, graph theory, algebraic geometry, additive combinatorics, and quantum optics.

My Notes

  • The base model matters more than the orchestration: the basic generate-and-verify loop (A) solved all nine Erdős problems on its own. Adding AlphaProof (B) mostly matched it within the margin of error, and the full-featured agent (D) beat them only on the hardest instances (#138 and #125, 2–5x cheaper there) while running about twice as expensive on the rest. Standalone AlphaProof and versions of (A) built on smaller Gemini models solved nothing. The capability comes from the frontier prover, not the evolutionary machinery around it, because the Lean compiler already supplies a hard correctness signal. Co-Scientist [2] is the opposite case: with no compiler to check its hypotheses, its Elo tournament is the only quality signal it has, so the same machinery that is optional here becomes essential.

  • Humans still formalize the problem and digest the proof: the agent only starts once someone has written the conjecture as a Lean theorem, and its output is a machine-checked proof that still has to be read back out (“deformalized”) and understood. It is the split Terence Tao named: generation and verification race ahead while digestion lags. It also revives the older question of what mathematicians are for once a machine can write the proof.

  • Known answers versus open problems: the Leipzig benchmark [3] graded models on 100 research-level questions that already had known answers, leaving only two unsolved after three rounds. This paper instead targets open problems with no known answer, where a result counts only when the Lean compiler accepts the proof.

  • A price tag on open problems: a few hundred dollars to settle a question open for decades makes attempting a conjecture a budgeting decision. Progress now has a unit cost, so you can buy more of it, like the broader automation of AI R&D. The bottleneck remains human bandwidth: formalizing the problems and digesting the proofs.

References

  1. Tsoukalas, George, Kovsharov, Anton, Shirobokov, Sergey, Surina, Anja, Firsching, Moritz, Bérczi, Gergely, Ruiz, Francisco J. R., Suggala, Arun, Wagner, Adam Zsolt, Wieser, Eric, Yu, Lei, Huang, Aja, Horváth, Miklós Z., Ferrauiolo, Andrew, Michalewski, Henryk, Grosu, Codrut, Hubert, Thomas, Balog, Matej, Kohli, Pushmeet, and Chaudhuri, Swarat. “Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.22763), May 21, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22763
  2. Gottweis, Juraj, Weng, Wei-Hung, Daryin, Alexander, and 48 co-authors. “Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y
  3. Balakin, Andrei, Bóna, Miklós, Brandenburg, Marie-Charlotte, and 46 co-authors. “Benchmarks in Leipzig.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.05818), June 4, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05818

Related Posts

  • An OpenAI Model Disproves a Discrete-Geometry Conjecture: the informal counterpart, an Erdős conjecture settled by a general model and checked by a human committee rather than a compiler.
  • Even Experts Are Surprised by AI’s Latest ‘Vibe-Mathing’ Advance: another AI result on a long-open math problem, with the value in a transferable technique rather than the single proof.
  • Math Is AGI: Carina Hong on Axiom and Formal Reasoning: the same bet that formal, machine-checkable proof is the path for AI mathematics.
  • The Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics: the governance counterpart, asking for human oversight of AI in mathematical research.

item.title: Robin: A Multi-Agent System That Ran the Whole Discovery Loop
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery [1] (Nature, May 2026), Ali Essam Ghareeb and Benjamin Chang (co-first authors), jointly supervised by Andrew D. White, Michaela M. Hinks, and Samuel G. Rodriques, with nine co-authors from FutureHouse, the University of Oxford, and Fordham University, introduce Robin, a system of bird-named agents that runs an experimental-biology project end to end: it reads the literature, proposes hypotheses, designs experiments, and analyzes the data that comes back.

Scientific discovery is driven by the iterative process of observation, hypothesis generation, experimentation, and data analysis. Despite recent advancements in applying artificial intelligence to biology, no system has yet automated all these stages. Here, we introduce Robin, the first multi-agent system capable of fully automating both hypothesis generation and data analysis for experimental biology. By integrating literature search agents with data analysis agents, Robin can generate hypotheses, propose experiments, interpret experimental results, and generate updated hypotheses, achieving a semi-autonomous approach to scientific discovery. By applying this system, we were able to identify promising therapeutic candidates for dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD), the major cause of blindness in the developed world. Robin proposed enhancing retinal pigment epithelium phagocytosis as a therapeutic strategy, and identified and confirmed in vitro efficacy for ripasudil and KL001. Ripasudil is a clinically-used Rho kinase (ROCK) inhibitor that has never previously been proposed for treating dAMD. To elucidate the mechanism of ripasudil-induced upregulation of phagocytosis, Robin then proposed and analyzed a follow-up RNA-seq experiment, which revealed upregulation of ABCA1, a lipid efflux pump and possible novel target. All hypotheses, experimental directions, data analyses, and data figures in the main text of this report were produced by Robin. As the first AI system to autonomously discover and validate novel therapeutic candidates within an iterative lab-in-the-loop framework, Robin establishes a new paradigm for AI-driven scientific discovery.

Methods

Robin coordinates three specialized bird-named agents, with a human running the wet-lab steps in between. It is semi-autonomous by design: humans execute the experiments and review the ranked candidates, and every hit is treated as a hypothesis that still needs standard pre-clinical and clinical validation.

  • The agents are split by job. Crow and Falcon are literature-search agents — Crow runs concise searches, Falcon deep ones — with access to the scientific literature, clinical-trial reports, and the Open Targets Platform. Finch is the data-analysis agent, writing and running its own code in a Jupyter notebook to analyze flow-cytometry and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data. Robin is not a single model: Crow and Falcon run on OpenAI’s o4-mini to synthesize what they retrieve, while Anthropic’s Claude 3.7 Sonnet serves as the ranking judge and as Finch’s base model.
  • The loop. Given only a disease name, Robin uses Crow to propose candidate mechanisms, each paired with an in vitro model to test it, ranks those reports, and runs the top one as its assay (a lab test that measures a specific biological activity). Falcon then evaluates drug candidates, ranked by the strength of the scientific rationale, the pharmacological profile, and the quality of the supporting literature. Ranking is pairwise: the LLM judge compares reports two at a time (round-robin for 25 or fewer, otherwise 300 sampled pairs), and a Bradley-Terry-Luce model — the standard way to turn pairwise win/loss records into a single strength score per item — produces the ranking. A human runs the top picks in the lab, Finch analyzes the returned data, and Robin interprets the result to seed the next round.
  • Consensus over many analysis runs. Because reading biological data is ambiguous and the agents are stochastic, Finch runs several independent analysis trajectories and a meta-analysis reconciles them into a consensus before Robin acts on it.
  • Throughput. Robin analyzed 551 papers in about 30 minutes against an estimated 540 hours for a human, roughly a 200-fold reduction over running the workflow by hand.

Results

The team pointed Robin at dry AMD as a proof of concept.

  • Robin picked a phagocytosis assay and ran the screen. From an initial review of 151 papers it proposed boosting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytosis and chose that assay over four alternatives (Figure 2a), then read about 400 more papers to rank 30 drug candidates. The assay doses cells, adds pH-sensitive (pHrodo) beads, and reads uptake by flow cytometry (2b); Finch wrote the gating code to isolate live single cells (2c–e) and scored each drug’s fold-change in fluorescence against a DMSO (solvent) control, where the Rho-kinase (ROCK) inhibitor Y-27632 came out significant (2f). Plainly: the cells that keep the retina clean normally swallow up debris; Robin bet that helping them do more of it would treat the disease, built a dish test for that swallowing, and found a compound (Y-27632) that boosted it.
  • A follow-up RNA-seq experiment pointed at ABCA1. To explain why Y-27632 worked, Robin proposed sequencing treated RPE cells. Finch’s differential-expression analysis found a 3-fold upregulation of ABCA1, a lipid efflux pump (Figure 3b), agreed across most of its analysis trajectories (3c), with gene-ontology (GO) enrichment in actin-filament organization, small-GTPase signaling, and autophagy (3d) — consistent with a cytoskeletal route to the phagocytic boost. Plainly: to learn why that compound helped, Robin read which genes the treated cells switched on, and a fat-transport gene called ABCA1 stood out — hinting that the cells’ internal scaffolding is what changed.
  • Ripasudil outperformed Y-27632 and validated in primary cells. In a second round Robin proposed ripasudil, a ROCK inhibitor approved for glaucoma in Japan and never before proposed for dAMD (Figure 4a). It raised phagocytosis 1.89-fold over DMSO (4b) and was more potent than Y-27632 in a dose-response (4c). Re-screening in stem-cell-derived primary human RPE confirmed both as hits, ripasudil again the stronger (4d–e), alongside KL001, a circadian-clock modulator. Plainly: next Robin proposed ripasudil, an existing glaucoma drug, which worked even better and kept working in real human cells — as did KL001, a drug that acts on the body clock.
  • Ablations confirmed the literature search mattered. Stripping the retrieval out from under Crow and Falcon — leaving the same o4-mini model to answer on its own — drove hallucinated references from 0% to 44.5%, and OpenAI’s Deep Research, given the same prompt, generated candidates that produced no hits in the assay [1]. Plainly: when the same model had to work without Robin’s literature tools, it invented fake references and its drug picks failed — the careful reading was what made the difference.

My Notes

  • Robin and Co-Scientist refine hypotheses in opposite directions. Google’s Co-Scientist [2] improves its hypotheses internally and scales their quality with more test-time compute, but the quality signal is the model scoring its own debates — an internal-consistency measure, with experimental validation left to humans. Robin improves them externally instead, feeding Finch’s analysis of real wet-lab data back into the next round. The improvement is anchored to different things: for Co-Scientist, a self-evaluated score; for Robin, experimental results. By the Robin paper’s own framing, analyzing those results and re-hypothesizing on them is the step prior systems, Co-Scientist among them, did not automate [1].

  • Grounding the literature search is what mattered. Robin’s own ablations are the clearest evidence: strip the retrieval out and the references hallucinate, swap in a general-purpose research agent and the drug picks all miss in the assay. Co-Scientist relied on the same move: its Reflection agent called external search to hold implausible hypotheses down. Two independently built systems converged on literature-grounded retrieval over a bare general model.

References

  1. Ghareeb, Ali Essam, Chang, Benjamin, Mitchener, Ludovico, Yiu, Angela, Szostkiewicz, Caralyn J., Shved, Dmytro, Gyimesi, Gavin J., Laurent, Jon M., Wright, Samantha M., Razzak, Muhammed T., White, Andrew D., Finnemann, Silvia C., Hinks, Michaela M., Rodriques, Samuel G. “A multi-agent system for automating scientific discovery.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10652-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10652-y
  2. Gottweis, Juraj, Weng, Wei-Hung, Daryin, Alexander, Tu, Tao, et al. “Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist.” Nature (DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y), May 19, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y

Related Posts

  • A Deep Learning Approach to Antibiotic Discovery: the AI-drug-discovery precedent Robin extends, from screening molecules to an agent that forms the hypothesis, designs the assay, and validates dry-AMD candidates.
  • MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems: the failure modes, including weak verification and inter-agent misalignment, that Robin’s consensus trajectories, human-in-the-loop checks, and retrieval grounding are built to avoid.
  • Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies: treats the agent topology itself as the thing to optimize, where Robin instead fixes a hand-designed topology and grounds it in wet-lab feedback.
  • Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?: the case for automating the research pipeline, with Robin a data point on the science side that automates hypothesis search and analysis while humans run the lab.

item.title: Co-Scientist: Gemini Agents That Generate and Rank Hypotheses
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist [1] (Nature, May 2026), Juraj Gottweis, Wei-Hung Weng, Alexander Daryin, Tao Tu, and five other co-first authors, with senior authors including Vivek Natarajan, Demis Hassabis, James Manyika, Yossi Matias, and Pushmeet Kohli, and roughly 50 co-authors across Google DeepMind, Google Research, Google Cloud AI Research, Stanford University School of Medicine, Houston Methodist, and Imperial College London, introduce Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based system that proposes research hypotheses and ranks them in a tournament that improves the survivors.

Scientific discovery is driven by scientists generating novel hypotheses for complex problems that undergo rigorous experimental validation. To augment this process, we introduce Co-Scientist, a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini for structured scientific thinking and hypothesis generation. Co-Scientist aims to help scientists discover new original knowledge. Conditioned on their research objectives and prior scientific evidence, it formulates demonstrably novel research hypotheses for experimental verification. The system’s design involves agents continuously generating, critiquing and refining hypotheses accelerated by scaling test-time compute. Key contributions include: (1) a multi-agent architecture with an asynchronous task execution framework for flexible compute scaling; (2) a tournament evolution process for self-improving hypotheses generation. Automated evaluations show continued benefits of test-time compute scaling, improving hypothesis quality over time. While general purpose, we focus the validation in three biomedical applications: drug repurposing, novel target discovery, and explaining mechanisms of anti-microbial resistance. Specifically, Co-Scientist helped identify new drug repurposing candidates and synergistic combination therapies for acute myeloid leukemia, which were validated through in vitro experiments. These real-world validations demonstrate the potential of Co-Scientist to accelerate scientific discovery and usher in an era of AI empowered scientists.

Methods

Co-Scientist is a compound, multi-agent system built on Gemini, run as a “scientist in the loop”: a researcher states a goal in natural language, sets constraints, and can steer the search or seed hypotheses as it works. The system generates and ranks hypotheses, but the experimental validation stays with people: every proposal passes human expert review and wet-lab assays before it is confirmed.

  • Six specialized agents under a supervisor. A Supervisor agent parses the goal and assigns six worker agents (Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review) to an asynchronous task queue, all sharing a persistent context memory. The agents are not separate models: they all run on the same base LLM (Gemini 2.0 here) and differ only by their prompts, and the framework is model-agnostic. Every hypothesis must meet default criteria: plausibility, novelty, testability, and safety.
  • Grounding and critique. The Generation agent drafts hypotheses from literature search and simulated scientific debate. The Reflection agent then reviews them as a peer reviewer would, and its access to web search and specialized AI models is what kept hallucinated, implausible hypotheses down.
  • Fitness is winning debates. Hypotheses are scored by an internal Elo rating — the chess-style score that ranks competitors, here hypotheses, by who wins pairwise matchups. The Ranking agent stages those matchups as multi-turn scientific debates (single-turn for lower-ranked pairs), judged on correctness, novelty, and testability. A new hypothesis enters at an Elo of 1200 and climbs or falls by its record. The Proximity agent clusters similar hypotheses so the debates pit close rivals against each other.
  • Evolution reproduces rather than overwrites. The Evolution agent builds new hypotheses from the top-ranked ones: combining the strongest parts of several (the crossover analog), spinning off variants inspired by one or more parents, regrounding them in fresh literature, simplifying them, or forcing deliberately divergent “out-of-the-box” ideas (the mutation analog). It never edits a hypothesis in place, so strong parents survive and every offspring has to earn its own Elo back in the tournament.
  • It improves without retraining. A Meta-review agent distills recurring weaknesses from the reviews and debates and appends that feedback to every agent’s prompt on the next round, so the system learns by updating its context rather than its weights, with no fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. An asynchronous framework lets it spend more test-time compute on a goal, with the Supervisor tracking progress through periodic summary statistics and deciding when a run hits a terminal state. There is no convergence threshold: quality (Elo) never saturated in the paper’s runs, so they ended on a compute budget rather than because the system stopped improving.

Results

The paper validates Co-Scientist with automated benchmarks and end-to-end wet-lab experiments in three biomedical areas, all run with experts in the loop. [1]

  • Quality climbs with test-time compute. Across 203 research goals, both the average and best Elo ratings rose the longer the system reasoned, with no sign of saturation.
  • Beats frontier reasoning models. On 15 expert-curated goals, Co-Scientist’s Elo eventually surpassed Gemini 2.0 Pro and Flash Thinking, OpenAI o1 and o3-mini-high, and DeepSeek R1.
  • Experts preferred its output. On 11 goals, Co-Scientist scored an average preference rank of 2.36 and novelty and impact ratings of 3.64 and 3.09 out of 5, and was the top pick of all four LLM judges.
  • AML drug repurposing. Co-Scientist generated repurposing hypotheses across a curated list of 2,300 approved drugs spanning 34 cancer types. After expert oncologists reviewed and ranked its predictions, five candidates were tested in vitro, and three (binimetinib, pacritinib, cerivastatin) inhibited acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cell viability. Binimetinib, approved for metastatic melanoma, reached a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50, the dose that cuts cell survival in half, so lower means more potent) as low as 2 nM in all AML lines but NOMO-1, while leaving a non-leukemia control line largely unharmed.
  • Novel single-agent candidates. With no prior preclinical evidence or human feedback, Co-Scientist proposed three wholly new picks: nanvuranlat, KIRA6, and leflunomide. KIRA6, which blocks a cellular stress sensor (the enzyme IRE1α), had an 18-fold safety margin: it killed the stem-cell-like KG-1a leukemia cells at one-eighteenth the dose that affected healthy control cells (an IC50 of 10 nM against 180 nM).
  • Synergistic combinations. Co-Scientist also proposed multi-drug regimens, and of seven it suggested, the two- and three-drug combinations were mostly synergistic in one leukemia line (MOLM-13), meaning the drugs together killed more cells than the sum of each alone, while the harder-to-treat KG-1a line responded inconsistently.
  • Liver fibrosis and antimicrobial resistance. In lab-grown mini-livers (hepatic organoids), Co-Scientist proposed three epigenetic targets (genes that switch other genes on or off), and drugs against two of them reduced scarring without harming the tissue (one, vorinostat, is already an approved cancer drug). For antimicrobial resistance, it worked out in about two days how a family of mobile DNA elements that ferry resistance genes between bacteria (cf-PICIs) jump across species, by borrowing the tail proteins of different viruses, matching an unpublished experiment that was running at the same time.

My Notes

  • Both Nature papers point to the same lesson: grounding beats the raw model. Co-Scientist’s own ablation found that giving the Reflection agent access to external search tools is what prevented hallucinated, implausible hypotheses [1] — the gains came from disciplined literature retrieval rather than a bigger base model. FutureHouse’s Robin [2], in Nature the same week, reached the comparable conclusion automating discovery for macular degeneration. Two independently built systems converged on this.

  • The Elo curve is self-evaluated. It is scored by the same model that generates the hypotheses, so a rising Elo means later hypotheses beat earlier ones in the model’s own debates — an internal-consistency signal that can optimize for what the judge likes rather than what is true.
